intro: At the centre of Kinderszenen, a quiet piano melody keeps reaching a little higher. Träumerei is only twenty-four written bars; each phrase seems reluctant to end.

sections.label: A · A melody rising from C
B · E♭ darkens the rising tune
A′ · F major, then a long farewell
sections.mNote: A high A pauses under a fermata before the close

cues.title: C reaches up to F
cues.text: A single C rises to F and waits. Then the melody climbs again, towards the F an octave above. Underneath, the other voices move slowly, each with a line of its own.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, p. 11, bars 1–4; pitches confirmed in Ying-Chun Liu’s Mutopia transcription. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/fe/IMSLP03060-Schumann-Op015Brt6016.pdf
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Schumann’s little thing
cues.text: Saturday, 24 February 1838. In his diary Schumann records composing “the little thing Träumerei”. The following evening he is back at another Kinderszene in F major, which strikes him as “very pretty”.
cues.evidence: Schumann’s diary, 24–25 February 1838, quoted in Thomas Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), item 1. Translations of “das kleine Ding” and “die mir sehr hübsch vorkommt”. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

cues.title: Thirty little droll things
cues.text: On 17 March 1838 Schumann tells Clara that he has written “some thirty small droll things” and chosen about twelve for his Kinderszenen. She will enjoy them, he promises, though she will have to forget herself as a virtuoso.
cues.evidence: Schumann to Clara Wieck, Leipzig, 17 March 1838, Jugendbriefe (1885), p. 277, quoted in Thomas Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), item 3: “an die 30 kleine putzige Dinger … von denen ich etwa zwölf ausgelesen”; our translation. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf Same letter, same sentences, in May Herbert’s English translation, Early Letters of Robert Schumann (1888), pp. 264–265: “about thirty quaint little things, from which I have selected twelve”. https://archive.org/details/earlylettersofro010823mbp

cues.title: Left out of the early programmes
cues.text: When Marie Wieck plays six of the pieces in Dresden on 18 January 1853, Träumerei is not among them. In Vienna on 17 March 1857, Clara’s pupil Nanette Falk plays three, all from Marie’s list, so it misses that programme too.
cues.evidence: Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), items 15 and 16: the Dresden programme of 18 January 1853 and the Vienna programme of 17 March 1857. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

cues.title: The first F returns
cues.text: The opening F returns after the middle passage’s excursions through G minor and D minor. Schumann restores the first phrase almost exactly. Later, a high A is held under a fermata, and the final descent stretches out with a ritardando.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 11, bars 9–24: G-minor and D-minor cadences, return at bar 17, fermata on A in bar 22 and final ritardando.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Pictures, poems and a film
cues.text: In 1877 Friederike Medem publishes silhouettes with verses for four of the pieces, Träumerei among them. A Leipzig edition of 1886 pairs the music with poems by Albert Träger and pictures by Alexander Zick. In 1943–44 UFA makes a film called Träumerei.
cues.evidence: Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), items 17, 33–34 and 38: the Zick and Träger edition, the UFA film Träumerei and the Medem silhouettes. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

transitions.title: The upbeat starts another dream
transitions.from: A · A melody rising from C
transitions.how: The eighth bar slows onto C-major harmony, the dominant of F. A low C in the melody becomes the pickup back to F, while the bass settles beneath it on F. The repeat begins with the same quiet upward reach.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 11, bar 8 and the repeat to bar 1; final C-major harmony confirmed in the Mutopia transcription.

transitions.title: The climb reaches E♭
transitions.to: B · E♭ darkens the rising tune
transitions.how: The new phrase begins on F over an F bass, just like the opening. Its climb now reaches E♭, and the inner parts lead towards G minor. Four bars later the whole rising shape starts again on B♭, with B♭ in the bass.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 11, bars 9–14; E♭ at bar 10, G-minor cadence at bar 12 and B♭ phrase at bar 13.

transitions.title: D minor releases the opening F
transitions.from: B · E♭ darkens the rising tune
transitions.to: A′ · F major, then a long farewell
transitions.how: The middle phrase comes to rest in D minor and slows. A small grace-note C leads up to the opening F; beneath it, a low F restores the home key. The tune begins its first phrase again.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 11, bars 16–17; grace note and bass pitches checked against the Mutopia transcription.

fields.note: The sources do not say which printed edition Donald Betts played from. Schumann’s Kinderszenen exist in a pre-publication printing, the 1839 first edition and its revised second issue, and Clara Schumann’s later edition; the recording is not matched to any of them here.

composer.epithet: A bookseller’s son who put lovers, masks and arguments into piano music, and made criticism a form of friendship.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The books offered twins, disguises, conversations that wandered away from their subject and returned by an unexpected door. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The music changes partners every few bars.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828, moved to Heidelberg the following year, and finally persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil who had much to catch up on. By 1832, paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and began building a life at the writing desk.
